tweets.text: RT @ethvisionorg: Several issues exist: 1. The statement that "if the staked ETH exceeds a certain threshold, such as 50%, it will create a strong incentive for the remaining 50% to stake to avoid dilution" is unfounded; it's only one possibility. In reality, as the staking ratio increases, the staking yield gradually decreases. The current surge in staking is largely due to the prolonged low price of ETH (which is also just one factor). The staking ratio is a complex factor, not a simple 0 or 1 model. 2. The statement that "holding a high proportion of $ETH staked will introduce many problems and act as a centralized force" is also unfounded. LSTs' value is entirely rooted in ETH. If ETH is decentralized, then LSTs are unlikely to become a centralized force. Because if LSTs try to undermine ETH, they will perish simultaneously. 3. The statement that "LSTs with a large ETH staking ratio will introduce tail risk because they become too big to fail. In the event of a major leak, the chain may be forced to fork" sounds correct, but strictly speaking... Any project/DApp that grows large will face the same risks. Even Ethereum's own code may have bugs. Presuming LSTs guilty based on theoretical possibilities demonstrates ignorance of law and common sense. 4. Vitalik and his core group have long been wary of LSTs like Lido because LSTs are not an unexpected bonus of the free market designed by EF. Those around Vitalik are deeply concerned that the growing influence of LSTs will weaken their own, so they are attempting to "reduce power" by addressing top-level rules. This is a typical power struggle, not a purely technical issue. In reality, L2s pose a much greater threat to Ethereum, and Vitalik, due to his deep involvement in L2s design, only acknowledged the problem this year. 5. My view is that Ethereum's current monetary policy and issuance curve do not have real problems. LSTs are a spontaneous market outcome and are part of Ethereum's greatness. Trying to change a problem that isn't a problem is itself a problem. Ethereum is already a massive economy worth hundreds of billions of dollars; the stability of its monetary policy is a prerequisite for its long-term consensus building. The large number of left-wing individuals within Ethereum (EF) excels in philosophy and theory but lacks substantial practical experience and product development mindset. This poses a threat to Ethereum to some extent, and the very proposal of this EIP exposes this problem. The near-universal opposition to this absurd proposal from the community also serves as a check and balance. Ethereum remains great, but not because of a few individuals. Ethereum doesn't need heroes; some should voluntarily step aside.

tweets.text: Statutory interpretation (like admin law 😊) was one of my favorite subjects in law school. The statutory canon against absurdity is an actual statutory canon! dating back to a Supreme Court case from 1868. It’s not invoked often and has been controversial bc it can require courts to depart from a statute’s literal reading, which some people are very offended by. But yes it is real. (Also that case was about a sheriff who arrested a mailman who had been indicted for murder; the court ruled that the sheriff couldn’t be prosecuted for violating a federal law that made it illegal to “obstruct the mail” because that’s obviously not what Congress meant. tweets.text: RT @Artem_Oak: Not speaking as a solo staker, but rather as someone who has been part of the Ethereum ecosystem for a while and that is aware of what's at stake here Our full opinion is available below, but here are some personal thoughts: 1 - The risks outweigh the benefits Network disruption, uncertainty, DeFi implosion, LST premium, and a bunch of other factors make me think that this is not the right way forward. I don't think this proposal comes from malicious actors, but feels like the people behind it still view Ethereum like we are in 2021. Ethereum has grown and is larger than a simple tech layer. You have to take it into consideration. I think @StaniKulechov had some really good points there (other opinions are also included in the article). 2 - Solo stakers and the centralisation issue Let's imagine for a second that this goes through. Solo stakers will be the ones who will need monitoring the staking curve, will bear the most costs, will capture less MEV and priority fees, will take on most of the risks. Good points by @mzeller on this. 3 - Don't understand why it is done now Yes, the staking has become popular among institutions, LST providers, and actors like @BitMNR who launched its own $ETH staking service. Why would you want, as Ethereum battles for adoption & relevance, try and change the most interesting part about owning ETH today? It feels like a state of urgency that doesn't need to be one. I would love to hear the opinion from @ethlabs_org on this EIP in general to see if we are wrong to disagree with the timing or if it's something that should not be the priority today (gm @barnabemonnot) Overall take (as someone who is an $ETH believer, not a solo staker), this proposal creates a lot of uncertainty, could become a real pain to manage both for solo stakers, but also institutions, while Ethereum seems to finally gain traction and get in front of its competitors. Please read the whole article that recaps everything around the proposal, the opinions of those who support it and who are against it, and overall a really good read by @MaximilienP51 with comments from @_prenomnom_ and myself.
